source_text: Καὶ περὶ μὲν τοῦ παρ’ Ἑβραίων τὰ τῶν φιλοσόφων ἐσκευωρῆσθαι δόγματα μικρὸν ὕστερον διαληψόμεθα, πρότερον δέ, ὅπερ ἀκόλουθον ἦν, περὶ τῶν κατὰ Μωυσέα χρόνων ἤδη λεκτέον, δἰ ὧν δειχθήσεται ἀναμφηρίστως πάσης σοφίας ἀρχαιοτάτη ἡ κατὰ Ἑβραίους φιλοσοφία. εἴρηται μὲν οὖν περὶ τούτων ἀκριβῶς Τατιανῷ ἐν τῷ Πρὸς Ἕλληνας, εἴρηται δὲ καὶ Κασσιανῷ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ τῶν Ἐξηγητικῶν· ἀπαιτεῖ δὲ ὅμως τὸ ὑπόμνημα καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐπιδραμεῖν τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον εἰρημένα. Ἀπίων τοίνυν ὁ γραμματικός, ὁ Πλειστονίκης ἐπικληθείς, ἐν τῇ τετάρτῃ τῶν Αἰγυπτιακῶν ἱστοριῶν, καίτοι φιλαπεχθημόνως πρὸς Ἑβραίους διακείμενος, ἅτε Αἰγύπτιος τὸ γένος, ὡς καὶ κατὰ Ἰουδαίων συντάξασθαι βιβλίον, Ἀμώσιος τοῦ Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέως μεμνημένος καὶ τῶν κατ’ αὐτὸν πράξεων, μάρτυρα παρατίθεται Πτολεμαῖον τὸν Μενδήσιον. καὶ τὰ τῆς λέξεως αὐτοῦ ὧδε ἔχει· κατέσκαψε δὲ τὴν Ἀουαρίαν Ἄμωσις κατὰ τὸν Ἀργεῖον γενόμενος Ἴναχον, ὡς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις ἀνέγραφεν ὁ Μενδήσιος Πτολεμαῖος. ὁ δὲ Πτολεμαῖος οὗτος ἱερεὺς μὲν ἦν, τὰς δὲ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέων πράξεις ἐν τρισὶν ὅλαις ἐκθέμενος βίβλοις κατὰ Ἄμωσίν φησιν Αἰγύπτου βασιλέα Μωυσέως ἡγουμένου γεγονέναι Ἰουδαίοις τὴν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου πορείαν, ἐξ ὧν συνῶπται κατὰ Ἴναχον ἠκμακέναι τὸν Μωσέα. παλαίτατα δὲ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν τὰ Ἀργολικά, τὰ ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου λέγω, ὡς Διονύσιος ὁ Ἁλικαρνασσεὺς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις διδάσκει, τούτων δὲ † τεσσαράκοντα μὲν γενεαῖς νεώτερα τὰ Ἀττικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Κέκροπος τοῦ διφυοῦς δὴ καὶ αὐτόχθονος, ὥς φησι κατὰ λέξιν ὁ Τατιανός, ἐννέα δὲ τὰ Ἀρκαδικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Πελασγοῦ·
pass_a_gloss: And concerning the fact that the doctrines of the philosophers were seen among the Hebrews, we will speak a little later, but first, as was fitting, we must speak about the times of Moses, through which it will be shown clearly that the Hebrew philosophy is the most ancient of all wisdom. For Tatian has spoken accurately about these things in his work Against the Greeks, and also Cassian has spoken in the first of his Exegetical works; however, the memorandum also demands that we run through the things said according to the place. Apion the grammarian, who was called Plistonicus, in the fourth of his Egyptian histories, although he was hostile towards the Hebrews, being an Egyptian by race, and having even composed a book against the Jews, mentions Amosis, king of the Egyptians, and the events that occurred during his reign, and presents Ptolemaeus of Mendes as a witness. And the words of the latter are as follows: Amosis, having become Inachus according to the Argive account, dug up Auaria, as Ptolemaeus of Mendes wrote in his Chronicles. This Ptolemaeus was a priest, and having set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings in three whole books, says that during the reign of Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews made their journey out of Egypt under the leadership of Moses, from which it is clear that Moses flourished during the time of Inachus. But the most ancient of the Greek accounts are the Argolic ones, which I call the ones from Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his Chronicles, and of these, the Attic accounts, which are from Cecrops, who was two-natured and autochthonous, as Tatian says word for word, are forty generations newer, and the Arcadian accounts, which are from Pelasgus, are nine newer.
pass_b_english: We will address a little later the question of whether the philosophers' doctrines were found among the Hebrews, but first, as is fitting, we must speak of the times of Moses, through which it will be demonstrated beyond dispute that the Hebrew philosophy is the most ancient of all wisdom. Tatian has already treated these matters accurately in his *Against the Greeks*, and Cassian has also done so in the first of his *Exegetical Works*; nevertheless, this memorandum requires us to run through the relevant statements in their proper place. Apion the grammarian, surnamed Plistonicus, in the fourth book of his *Egyptian Histories* — though hostile toward the Hebrews, being Egyptian by birth, and having even composed a book against the Jews — mentions Amosis, king of the Egyptians, and the events of his reign, and cites Ptolemaeus of Mendes as a witness. Ptolemaeus writes: "Amosis, who became Inachus in the Argive reckoning, dug up Avaris," as recorded in his *Chronicles*. This Ptolemaeus was a priest; having set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings in three complete books, he states that under Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews made their exodus from Egypt under the leadership of Moses, from which it follows that Moses flourished in the time of Inachus. The most ancient of the Greek traditions are the Argolic ones, those stemming from Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his *Chronicles*; and of these, the Attic traditions, which derive from Cecrops — who was two-natured and autochthonous, as Tatian says word for word — are forty generations later, while the Arcadian traditions, which derive from Pelasgus, are nine generations later.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex chronological arguments and the nested quotations of Apion and Ptolemaeus. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek. The translation of 'φιλαπεχθημόνως' as 'hostile' (Pass A) and 'hostile toward' (Pass B) correctly reflects the sense of the Greek, despite the unusual morphology. The distinction between the Argolic, Attic, and Arcadian generations is preserved.

The Greek text is accurately translated in Pass A and Pass B. The title 'Hebrew Philosophy and Chronology' correctly reflects the content. All proper nouns and names are consistently translated. The scriptural and historical references are preserved. No omissions or additions are present. The translation maintains the original meaning, including the nuances of negation, agency, and modality. The inline citations are correctly matched to the content. The text is complete and faithful to the source.
